sentences.text: Carinodens was an extinct genus of marine lizards from the Cretaceous period that belongs to the mosasaur family, measuring between 2 and 2.6 meters in length to make it one of the smallest known mosasaurs.

The name Carinodens means "keel teeth" and was established in 1969 as a replacement name for the previously used name Compressidens, reflecting its distinctive round, blunt teeth adapted for crushing primitive clams and oysters.
At just over two meters long, this animal stands as one of the smallest known members of the mosasaur family.
Dental wear evidence strongly suggests that the species C. belgicus ate hard-shelled benthic invertebrates.
The species C. fraasi was first described and illustrated by Louis Dollo in 1913 under the name Globidens fraasi.
Thurmond proposed the name Carinodens in 1969 as a substitute name because Compressidens was already used for a scaphopod mollusk.
The primary distinction between the species C. fraasi and C. belgicus is their dentition, with C. fraasi having unicuspid teeth and C. belgicus having tricuspid teeth.
Sharpe et al. (2024) suggested that the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — of Xenodens could not be distinguished from an earlier developmental stage of Carinodens.
Carinodens lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
Most cranial fossils of Carinodens come from the Netherlands and Belgium, while the only known postcranial material was found in Jordan.

Longrich et al. (2025) argued against synonymizing Xenodens with Carinodens, suggesting that significant differences in the maxilla and dentition make it unlikely that Xenodens is a juvenile Carinodens.
